# Page 2^page=2
Chain of command When dealing with issues, address them to your section editor. Continue up the line until you are satisfied with the results. Problems with the Editor-in-Chief should be ad- dressed to the adviser. Argonaut protocol states if you have a personal problem with someone on staff, your first attempt at communication is with that person. Conduct The Argonaut is a business. It sells advertising to make money for production costs and salaries. Advertising customers, campus and community officials and stu- dents will often be in and out of the office, so employees should act professionally. The Editor-in-Chief will deter- mine unprofessional behavior and may take disciplinary measures. Maintaining professionalism is a condition of employment. The The Editor-in-Chief is the ultimate arbiter on all newsroom matters. The adviser will oversee all activities, making appropriate recommendations and referring any personnel matters regarding theThe Editor- in-Chief ’s behavior or job performance to the Student Media Board. Only the Student Media Board may disci- pline the Editor-in-Chief. Sexual harassment Sexual harassment is unacceptable in any form. Sexual harassment of an employee or applicant is defined as unwelcome sexual advances, requests for sexual favors or other verbal or physical conduct of a sexual nature when: (a) submission to such conduct is made as a term or condi- tion of employment, promotion or status as an employee; (b) the person’s submission to or rejection of such conduct is used as a basis for a decision affecting that person or (c) such conduct has the purpose or effect of substantially interfering with the person’s work or work performance or creates a hostile or offensive environment. Moreover, an employee or applicant for employment is deemed to be a victim of sexual harassment if he or she is denied employ- ment, promotion or other employee benefit for which he or she is fully qualified, because someone else received pref- erential treatment in return for sexual favors. [UI Faculty Staff Handbook-3220 (Section B-2)] Alcohol and drugs It is a violation of University of Idaho Regent’s policy for any member of the faculty, staff or student body to jeopar- dize the academic operation or interests of UI by the use of alcohol or drugs. Sale or illegal possession or consumption of alcoholic beverages is prohibited in facilities owned, leased or operated by UI and on campus grounds. Alcoholic beverages may not be possessed or consumed under any circumstances in areas open to and most commonly used by the general pub- lic. These areas include but are not limited to lounges, student union buildings, recreation rooms, conference rooms, athletic facilities and other public areas of UI-owned buildings or grounds. Students who violate this policy are subject to sanc- tions established by UI (see 2300 VIII). Guests and visitors must observe these regulations while on campus or other UI property. Noncompliance may subject a person to sanctions imposed by UI as well as to the provisions of local and state law. [UI Faculty Staff Handbook-6340 (Section B)] Smoking Use of any tobacco product including cigarettes, cigars, pipes or any other product producing smoke is prohibited in all state-owned or state-leased buildings, facilities, ve- hicles or areas occupied by state employees. Smoking in a nonsmoking area is a violation and may result in discipline by a supervisor. Sanctions may range from warnings to dis- missal. The administrator or other employee with responsi- bility for a building, vehicle or work area is responsible for enforcing smoking policies in the building or work area. Vandalism In cases of vandalism, report information to the police so a report can be filed with UI. Phones Everyone on staff is required to answer Argonaut phones. Answer phones politely. It is appropriate to state your name and the area where the phone is located. For example, if answering the phone in the production area, you would say, “Argonaut production, this is [insert your name].” To transfer phone calls, press “flash,” then “5” plus the four-digit extension. Long distance access is available on the Editor-in-Chief’s phone. Use it only for Argonaut business. Inappropriate use of Argonaut phones is grounds for dismissal. Communication Effective and timely staff communication is essential to producing a quality newspaper. The Argonaut editors and adviser will communicate with staff via e-mail. Read all communications sent from your section editor, the manag- ing editor or Editor-in-Chief. The critique Adviser Tara Roberts will critique each edition of The Argonaut in two forms. The “redline” can be found posted on the newsroom bulletin board and will address typos, style and structure concerns and other technical issues. The critique itself is a written overview of all aspects of a given edition and will address specific areas of success and failure as well as journalism philosophy. Though your first point of contact and counsel should be with your section editors, Tara is always happy to go over work and offer ideas and thoughts. You can make an appointment, drop in to her of- fice or call her on her cell phone at (208) 310-0420.Argonaut Operations

Payroll Writers are paid by the story with a rate of pay assigned to a word count bracket. Photographers are paid for each published photo provided they properly save and write cap- tions for their photos. Management and editors are paid by stipend. In order to get paid, you must complete your W-9 and direct deposit information. You must fill out a pay sheet by noon on the last weekday of every month. Once completed in full detail, give the pay sheet to Tara Roberts or slide it under her door You will get paid once a month. Do not use the folder in the mailbox on Tara’s door. Payroll is time- sensitive, so turn in paysheets on time. The Argonaut assumes no liability for payroll complica- tions. The Argonaut reserves the right to make changes to the pay format and structure of the organization at any time. Also, failure to attend mandatory meetings may result in the loss of employment. The Argonaut does not guarantee any set rates of pay. The Argonaut only guarantees payment upon publication of material in The Argonaut. Argonaut rate of pay for 2017-2018 Stories and columns by staff writers: 0 - 255 words — $7 256 - 375 words — $11 376 - 1050 words — $15 1051 - 1355 words — $30 Over 1336 words — $45 Photos and videos: One photo — $10 Up to $20 for package Online galleries — $20 Videos — $15 Illustrations and graphics: $10-20 Production: Arg production — $35 per night Reading — $15 Argonaut Deadlines In order to produce The Argonaut, the deadline system must be observed so the newspaper will operate efficiently. Deadlines are not a suggestion. Failure to make deadline without notifying the appropriate section editor is not ac- ceptable. Reporters — Refer to section editor’s specific deadline Stories must be completed, spell-checked and submitted to your editor by 3 p.m. on the respective deadlines. The exemption to this policy is if the reporter must cover a time- sensitive or late-breaking story. The story can be turned in after the event after conferencing with your section editor. Illustrations — Refer to Art Director’s specific deadline Photographers — Refer to section editor’s specific dead- line Photos must be adjusted and saved into the appropriate folder. Before leaving the office, place cutlines (including ALL names, date and place of the event) into the “File info” section of the Photoshop file. Cutlines should follow AP style. Section editors — Refer to copy editor’s specific deadline Section editors should edit stories and promptly send them to copy editors via Facebook or email. If no copy editor is available, seciton editors may send stories to any other editor available at that time. Section editors must maintain a digital- first mindset and ensure stories have a quick turnaround online. Arg Production — 5 p.m. on Wednesdays Production has until 12 p.m. Wednesday to have the paper copy edited, designed and digitally sent to the Lewis- ton Tribune. Some holiday schedules may alter publication dates.Payroll and Deadlines

Story requirements 1. All stories must have a minimum of two sources. 2. All stories must meet the word count your editor sets. Usually this is no less than 500 words. 3. Stories need to have all facts double-checked by the writer before submission. Check names, dates, titles, etc. Turning in stories E-mail stories to your section editor. Files will be a .doc format, not .docx. The header will be as follows: Headline idea 1 Headline idea 2 Headline idea 3 Subhead idea Tag Writer name Argonaut Writing sample headlines helps the design staff work efficiently. Taking a few minutes to come up with at least two of varying length/word selection is a lot easier than the designer thinking of mediocre headlines for every story. The editing process 1. The writer turns the story in. 2. Section editor reads and edits story with track changes. 3. The story is e-mailed to the copy editor, who edits the story a second time. 4. The section editor accepts corrections, and places it in the production folder. 5. Production night: The designers put the story on the page. 6.Three readers edit the page to find more corrections. 7.The pages are given back to the paginators, who enter the final corrections. 6. When the pages are done, they’re sent to the printer in Lewiston. 7. As pages are being sent stories and photos are being uploaded to the website. 8. In the morning, there’s your byline and a story to be proud of. When your story is late: (By a few hours) The section editor gets a late start, in turn making the copy editor late, in turn making the page designers late, in turn making the page readers late, in turn sending the production staff home late. (By a whole day) By the time editing copy is done, the paginators are ready to work, but don’t have your story to work with. The page comes out late or incomplete. Your story may not get all of the time and tender loving care it needs, and we may have a lesser product. When your story is incomplete: The editor has to call you to get more information. Then you or your editor may have to do extra, last minute foot- work to make the story printable. Your story may not get printed. Refer to “late” for what happens when we have to wait for changes. Refer to “not turned in” for when we don’t print it. When you don’t turn your story in: The editor panics because she’s been planning for a week to include your story in the paper, and now must run wire (stuff The Arg didn’t write) to fill space. This also frustrates the paginators, who want to fill space with Arg copy to make the paper look good and read well — your story would have filled the space. So ... Please turn your stories in on time and complete. If you must be late or have trouble getting your story to length, let your editor know as soon as possible — not at deadline.Editing Process

Managing Editor The managing editor, as the title says, manages the newsroom. Keeping a close relationship with section editors, the managing editor helps to develop and follow stories, photos and pages in progress during Argonaut pro- duction. The managing editor reports any problems to the Editor-in-Chief. Other duties include: 1. Reviewing story assignments from news editor, making any additional story assignments if necessary. 2. Acts as the second read-out for all news stories before they go to the copy desk. 3. Assist Editor-in-Chief on production days. 4. Follow copy flow of all sections, keeping alert of what stories are in development and what problems there might be. 5. Coordinate material for all special sections or special topics in any given section. 6. Act as a liaison between advertising and editorial staff concerning special sections. 7. Work with section editors to make sure series are in print and future series in development. The managing editor also should make sure sections have at least one back-up feature (including art) that can be used at any time. 8. Take on any other responsibilities from the Editor-in- Chief. News Editor The news editor keeps a close relationship with the managing editor, developing and producing story ideas and keeping a pulse of campus news. Campus news always should be the No. 1 focus of the news section. The news editor should help writers develop strong reporting and writing skills, being a strong and stern editor who also gives aspiring writers encouragement and positive criti- cism. Main duties include: 1. Assigning stories to reporters, making sure there are enough stories to fill the news section in each issue. 2. Making sure writers adhere to deadlines. 3. Reading and editing writers’ stories, making appropriate edits to comply with AP and Argonaut style. Return stories to writers as necessary for further writing/reporting. 4. Present news story budget at huddle; coordinate with managing editor which stories will be on issue’s front page. 5. Properly and thoroughly fill out photo assignments and give to photo editor at huddle. Inform photo editor if a story is delayed or canceled. 6. Lead news staff meetings. 7. Be present in newsroom on production nights. 8. Read section proofs as they are completed. 9. Accept and complete any additional assignments from managing editor or Editor-in-Chief. Section Editors The section editors work in conjunction with the manag- ing editor to produce The Argonaut. Each section editor is responsible for developing the content and quality of their section. Each section editor shall assign stories to their reporters as well as proofread all stories before sending them to the copy desk. Section editors shall manage their staff in a professional and responsible manner. Section editors duties include: 1. Attend all editors’ meetings and weekly staff meetings. 2. Attend training sessions and workshops. 3. Produce an average of three stories a month. 4. Develop story ideas for staff members. 5. Actively pursue excellence in writing skills, accuracy and design in the section. 6. Complete photo assignment for photographers. 7. Supervise, motivate and train writers in story content and Argonaut policies. 8. Actively ensure stories are submitted by assigned dead- lines. Responsibly compile briefs and announcements for individual sections and produce special feature ideas. 9. Edit stories for factual, grammatical, style and spelling errors. 10. Refer ethical questions to the managing editor or Editor-in-Chief. 11. Attend production night fully to collaborate on page design and read final copy. 12. Cover important stories staff members are unable to write. 13. Write editorials and columns when assigned. 14. Follow Associated Press style. 15. Establish communication channels with other Argonaut staff members. 16. Maintain at least one office hour per week during busi- ness hours Monday through Friday. 17. Check mailbox daily. Check Argonaut e-mail account at least twice daily. 18. Answer telephones and assist callers promptly. 19. Use Argonaut equipment responsibly. 20. Display a professional attitude. 21. Take on additional duties as mutually agreed upon with the Editor-in-Chief.Staff Job Descriptions

Staff writers Staff writers produce most of what appears in the paper. Staff writers are also responsible for the following duties: 1. Research and write at least two stories per week. 2. Develop story ideas. 3. Follow Argonaut style and Associated Press style. 4. Spell-check document, and save story to appropriate folder by deadline. Always keep a backup of the story in case of technical errors. 5. Complete photo assignment information in the Google Docs to accompany story. 6. Check mailbox daily. 7. Answer telephone and assists callers promptly. 11. Use Argonaut equipment in a responsible manner. 12. Display a positive, professional attitude. 13. Meet all deadlines.Staff Job Descriptions

Termination of employment The ability to terminate employment of a staff member belongs to the particular section editor. These decisions must be approved by the Editor-in-Chief. Overview To seek truth and to publish it is the two-step goal of a journalist. To help journalists be true to this goal, newspa- pers, magazines and yearbooks adopt rules and guidelines — often called a code of ethics — for their members to follow. The code contains specific standards of conduct and moral judgments. Some points are specific and inflexible; others may be imprecise due to extenuating circumstances. Some are based on law. Once a code is adopted, it brings desirable unity to some degree in the group’s search for truth. The code answers questions and reminds those who operate under it that standards of honesty and performance exist. A code of ethics is not a burden; rather, a code is a useful license to practice newsgathering and publishing free of much uncer- tainty. The code can be used individually by men and women to measure their work. The code can also be used to evalu- ate the integrity of the publication as a consumer product. Readers should expect nothing less than the truth; adoption of a code of ethics by those who publish helps safeguard the public trust given to journalists. Argonaut Code of Ethics Free travel To remain free of influence or obligation to report a story, the journalist should not accept free travel, accommodations or meals while traveling. For convenience, sports reporters may travel on team charters, but the publication should pay the cost of transportation and related expenses. The same pay-as-you- go policy should apply to non-sports reporting as well, includ- ing businesses and governments. Free travel and accommoda- tions not related to a story or which a vendor may provide may be accepted if the primary purpose is for education or training and is related to the fulfillment of an agreement or contract. Gifts Gifts should not be accepted. Any gifts should be returned to the sender or sent to charity. If a gift is of no significant value, such as a desk trinket, small food item or pen, the staff member may retain the gift. Ownership of books, albums, other products given for review Any material given to the publication for review be- comes the property of the publication and not any indi- vidual staff member. Other employment Other employment must not conflict with the staffer’s first responsibilities to the publication. The staff member must report any other employment to the Editor-in-Chief to avoid any conflicts of interest with assignments or other staff editorial or business responsibilities or influences. Other off-campus or freelance media work Approval of work for an off-campus medium and freelance work should be sought in advance of the staff member’s commitment to The Argonaut. It is permissible only in a noncompetitive medium, on a staff member’s own time and should not conflict with the obligations to The Argonaut. Relationships and coverage Argonaut staff members must declare possible conflicts of interest and avoid involvement in stories in words, pho- tographs or artwork. Staff members must use good news judgment about family members or persons with whom they have a financial, adversarial or close relationship. Do not interview friends, family members or other Arg staff- ers for stories. Use of drugs/alcohol while on assignment Even though a staff member legally may be able to drink, no drinking (including light drinking) in a social setting such as a dinner or reception is allowed to avoid any suspicion by a source or the public that the staff mem- ber’s judgment, credibility or objectivity is impaired by alcohol. When covering an event where alcohol is served, staffers should not accept free drinks. Staff members should avoid the appearance they are being “wined and dined” by any source or agency. The use of illegal drugs while on assignment is abso- lutely prohibited, and is cause for immediate termina- tion. Plagiarism of words, art, other Plagiarism is prohibited. Plagiarism is defined as the word-for-word duplication of another person’s writing and shall be limited to passages that contain distinctively personal thoughts, uniquely stylized phrasing or exclu- sive facts. A comparable prohibition applies to the use of graphics and pictures. Information obtained from a pub- lished work must be independently verified before it can be reported as a new, original story. This policy also forbids lifting verbatim paragraphs from a wire service without attribution or pointing out that wire reports were used in compiling the story. Plagiarism is punishable by termina- tion of employment. Fabrication of any kind The use of composite characters or imaginary situations or characters is not allowed in news or feature stories. Fab- rication is grounds for immediate termination at the discre- tion of the Editor-in-Chief. A columnist may occasionally use such an approach in developing a piece, but it must be clear to the reader that the person or situation is fictional. Membership in campus organizations Staff members may not cover a campus organization they belong to or participate in any editorial or business decisions regarding that organization. However, staff members may provide story leads about the organizations to which they belong. Staff members should report their memberships to their section editor and Editor-in-Chief. To Argonaut Code of Ethics

maintain the role of the press as an independent watchdog of the government, a staff member should not be an elected or appointed member of student government. Use of photographs of victims of accidents, fires, natural disasters Photos have a tremendous impact on readers. The ques- tion of privacy vs. the public’s right to know should be considered. The line between good and bad taste and reality and sensationalism is not always easy to draw. Use caution and good judgment to maintain the dignity of the subject as much as possible without undermining the truth of the event. Reporting names, addresses of crime victims Staff members need to know the state laws that govern the publication of the names of rape and sexual assault victims. Generally the names of rape victims are not published. However, there is a trend to ask rape victims to go public. Victims of nonsexual crimes may be identified, but the publication has a responsibility to give some protection to the victim such as not listing full addresses. With the ex- ception of major crimes, an arrested person is not named until charges are filed. Profane, vulgar words, explicit sexual language, slang drug terms The primary audience of a college publication is adults. Profane and vulgar words are a part of everyday conversa- tion but not generally used for scholarly writing. During an interview, staff members may encounter interviewees who use words viewed as vulgar and profane. The writer may publish these words only if the words are important to the reader’s understanding of the situa- tion, the reality of life or if the words help establish the character of the interviewee. The writer may decide to limit references to prevent the vulgar or profane language from overshadowing the more important facts of the story. Profane and vulgar words are not acceptable for opinion writing. Though they may be vulgar or profane, individual words are not obscene. Explicit language — not vulgar, street language — describing sexual activities and human body parts and functions should be used for accurate reporting of health stories and in a more limited way, for sexual crime stories. Slang words or phrases used to describe drugs or the process of using drugs is not recommended. A section editor may consult with the Editor-in-Chief to deem appropriate usage of these terms. The Editor-in- Chief may approve or reject using any of these terms. Use of racial, ethnic or other group identifiers Identification of a person as a member of any popula- tion should be limited to those cases when that member- ship is essential for the reader’s complete understanding of the story. It should be done with great care so as not to perpetuate negative group stereotyping. When identifiers are used, it is important that the correct one be used. Some examples of identifiers: Hispanic, Jew, lesbian, Italian, person with AIDS (PWA), physically challenged, hearing impaired. False identity, stolen documents, concealed recording, eavesdropping In the ordinary course of reporting, no Argonaut em- ployee shall misrepresent himself as anything other than a representative of the publication. In extraordinary circum- stances when the Editor-in-Chief judges that information cannot be obtained in any other way and the value of that information is important, the editor may authorize other- wise. These cases are extremely rare. Staff members may not steal or knowingly receive stolen materials. Except in situations judged by the Editor-in-Chief as extraordinary, a staff member shall not record an interview or meeting with- out the interviewee’s permission or the obvious placement of a recording device (not hidden) at the start of the inter- view or meeting in which the interviewee or newsmaker do not object and are aware of the presence of the recording device. Committing an illegal act to eavesdrop on a source is not allowed. Check state laws on the use of recording devices for more information. Granting, preserving confidentiality to sources A reporter should not promise confidentiality to a source without the permission of the editor. The editor and reporter should know the laws pertaining to confidentiality and disclosure before a decision is made. A reporter should make every attempt to get the same information from another source who agrees to be named since the goal is to attribute all information to a specific source for all sources. Corrections An inaccuracy is never knowingly published. If any error is found, the publication is obligated to correct the error as soon as possible, regardless of the source of the error. A consistent location for the publication of correc- tions is recommended (Page 2). It should be clearly and prominently labeled as a correction. Ownership of work Regardless if a staff member is paid or is a volunteer, the publication owns the published and unpublished work done if the work was done as a staff assignment. Owner- ship of unpublished work may revert to the staff member at a certain time if the Editor-in-Chief agrees. The publi- cation has unlimited use of the work. The act of voluntari- ly joining a staff indicates approval of policy. Republished work will not be paid for subsequent uses. More on Ethics Reproduced from the Model Code of Ethics for Student Journalists from the Associated Collegiate Press, Copy-Argonaut Code of Ethics

right 1993. Defamation “Libel” involves the publishing of a falsehood that harms someone. Slander is the same doctrine applied to the spoken word. Collectively, they are referred to as “defamation.” Both are a matter of state laws, which usu- ally (not always) require that the falsehood be intentional. In New York Times v. Sullivan, the Supreme Court held that the First Amendment requires that before a public of- ficial can recover damages for a defamatory statement, he must prove it was made with “actual malice,” even if state laws otherwise allow recovery for negligent defamation. The Court has since expanded this to cover not only public officials but also “public figures” including individuals who involve themselves in controversies. Libel (Lat. libellus, a little book) A malicious publication by writing, printing, picture, effigy, sign or otherwise than by mere speech which exposes any living person (or the memory of any deceased person) to hatred, contempt, ridicule, obloquy, or which causes or tends to cause any person to be ashamed or avoided, or anything which has a tendency to injure any person, corporation, or association of persons, in his, her, or its business or occupation. A libel may be either a civil injury or a criminal of- fence. The theory upon which it is made the subject of criminal law is that it is calculated to cause a breach of the public peace. Libel differs essentially from slander in that it may be the subject of both criminal and civil litigation, whereas slander is not a criminal offence. Many statements may be actionable per se when writ- ten, printed or published which would not be actionable if merely spoken, without claiming and proving special damage. Thus unwritten words imputing immoral conduct are not actionable per se unless the misconduct imputed amounts to a criminal offence, for which the person slandered may be indicted. If the published matter holds a person up to public scorn, contempt, and ridicule, it is libellous per se. Libel per se embraces all cases that would be actionable if made orally and also embraces all other cases where the additional gravity imparted to the charge by the publication can fairly be supposed to make it dam- aging. To constitute libel there must be a publication, as well as in writing. While a defamatory writing is not libel if it remains with the writer undelivered, if it goes to other hands, even inadvertently, there has been a publication. The writing must go into the hands of persons who by knowledge of the language or of reading can become acquainted with its contents. In relation to criminal libel, it has been adjudged that even if the defamatory com- munication has been seen by no one but the person to whom it is addressed, a case has been made out, as in such an event it is likely to cause a breach of the public peace. [Barrow v. Lewellen, Hobart’s (K. B.) Reports, 62 a (152); Lyle v. Clason, 1 Cairnes (N. Y.), 581.] Argonaut Code of Ethics

Get your sources’ names. Get them right. Have them spell them to you, then spell back what you’ve written down. Here is why: •Source says, “My name is Jon Smyth.” •You hear: “My name is John Smith.” •You write: “John Smith said…” •Jon Smyth says, “My name isn’t John Smith, it’s Jon Smyth! Here is why: •You turn in a story that says “Bob Llama enjoys shooting people.” •Your editor goes “That can’t be right…” and calls you for clarification. •You say, “Well my notes are kind of messy, and it looks like people…” and since you don’t have con- tact information, you can’t check. •We print “Bob Llama enjoys shooting people,” when in fact he enjoys shooting pool. Incorrect punctuation can change the meaning of the sentence, the results of which can be far reaching. As writers, your byline is the one on the page. When readers see errors (even small ones) in your story, it reflects negatively on you because your name is what they see. It lowers your credibility as a journalist. A funeral is a service. 18. Head up. People do not head up committees. They head them. 19. Imply, infer. The speaker implies; the hearer infers. 20. In advance of, prior to. Use before; it sounds more natural. 21. It’s, its. Its is the possessive; it’s the contraction of it is. Wrong: What is it’s name? Right: What is its name? Its name is Fido. Right: It’s the first time she scored tonight. Right: It’s my coat. 22. Lay, lie. Lay is the action word; lie is the state of be- ing. Wrong: The body will lay in state until Wednesday. Right: The body will lie in state until Wednesday. Right: The prosecutor tried to lay the blame on him. However, the past tense of lie is lay. Right: The body lay in state from Tuesday until Wednesday. Wrong: The body laid in state from Tuesday until Wednesday. The past participle and the plain past tense of lay is laid. Right: She laid the pencil on the pad. Right: She had laid the pencil on the pad. Right: The hen laid the egg. 23. Less, fewer. If you can separate items in the quanti- ties being compared, use fewer. If not, use less. Wrong: The Rams are inferior to the Vikings because the have less good linemen. Right: The Rams are inferior to the Vikings because they have less experience. 24. Like, as. Do not use like for as or as if. In general, use like to compare with nouns and pronouns; use as when comparing with phrases and clauses that contain a verb. 25. Local place names. Kenworthy Performing Arts Cen- tre, Hartung Theatre, Kiva Theatre, Nuart Theater, Mos- cow Food Co-op, One World Cafe (no accent), Bucer’s Coffeehouse Pub, Wheatberries Bake Shop, Prichard Art Gallery, Wal-Mart/Wal-Mart Supercenter. 26. Marshall, marshal. Generally, the first form is correct only when the word is a proper noun: Susan Marshall. The second form is the verb form: She will marshal her forces. The second form is also the one to use for a title: fire mar- shal Cynthia Anderson, Field Marshal Erwin Rommel. 27. Mean, average, median. Use mean as synonymous with average. Both words refer to the sum of all compo- nents divided by the number of components. The median is the number that has as many components above it as below it. 28. Nouns as verbs. There is a trend toward using nouns as verbs. Resist it. Debut host, headquarters and author, for instance, are nouns, even though a dictionary may say they can be used as verbs. If you do so, you will come up with a monstrosity like: “Headquartered at her country home, Allison Doe hosted a party to celebrate the books she authored.” 29. Numbers. Numbers (other than ages, see above) are spelled out when they are single digits and numerals for 10 and above: There were nine people at the first day of class, but the instructor expected 20. There are some exceptions to this rule, check your stylebook if you aren’t sure. 30. Online examples. The Internet is downstyle, so is Web and Net. Web site is two words. Online is one word, not capitalized. Use blog, not Weblog. 31. Over, more than. They are not interchangeable. Over refers to spatial relationships: The plane flew over the city. More than is used with figures: More than 1,000 fans were in the crowd. 32. Oxford comma. Kill it. There is no comma before the preposition in a series. Ex: She likes eggs, bacon and toast for breakfast. 33. Parallel construction. Thoughts in series in the same Argonaut Style Guide

# Page 22^page=22
sentence require parallel construction. Wrong: The union demanded an increase of 10 percent in wages and to cut the work week to 35 hours. Right: The union demanded an increase of 10 percent in wages and a reduction in the work week to 35 hours. 34. Peddle, pedal. When selling something, you peddle it. When riding a bicycle or similar form of locomotion, you pedal it. 35. Principle, principal. A guiding rule or basic truth is a principle. The first, dominant or leading thing is principal. Principle is a noun; principal may be a noun or an adjec- tive. 36. Quotes. When introducing a speaker, “I like cheese,” said Bob Jones, 25, a sophomore. OR “I like cheese,” sophomore Bob Jones said. After the speaker’s been intro- duced: “I like cheese,” Jones said. Always use last name only after the source has been introduced once. Note the position of “said.” 37. Refute. The word connotes success in argument and almost always implies editorial judgment. Wrong: Father Williams refuted the arguments of the pro-abortion faction. Right: Father Williams responded to the arguments of the pro-abortion faction. 38. Reluctant, reticent. If someone does not want to act, that person is reluctant. If someone does not want to speak, that person is reticent. 39. Say, said. The most serviceable words in the journal- ist’s language are the forms of the verb to say. Let a person say something, rather than declare or admit or point out. Never let a person grin, smile, frown or giggle a quote. Said is the preferred word. Say often refers to a statement by a person or organization that can be considered con- sistent. (Ex. The company says is will continue to follow FCC regulations but no one was injured in the accident, Officer John Smith said.) 40. Slang. Do not try to use “with-it” slang. Usually a term is on the way out by the time we get it in print. 41. Temperatures. They may get higher or lower, but they do not get warmer or colder. Wrong: Temperatures are expected to warm up Friday. Right: Temperatures are ex- pected to rise Friday. 42. That, which. That tends to restrict the reader’s though and direct it the way you want it to go; which is nonrestric- tive, introducing a bit of subsidiary information. 43. Time, Date, Place. This is the correct order. Right: The event is 6 p.m., Sept. 1 in the Idaho Commons. Wrong: The event is in the Idaho Commons at 6 p.m. Sept. 1. 44. Under way, not underway. But do not say something got under way. Say it started or began. 45. Unique. Something that is unique is the only one of its kind. It cannot be very unique or quite unique or somewhat unique or rather unique. Do not use it unless you really mean unique. 46. Unnecessary words. Avoid them. Words like cur- rently, recently, also, both and that are often unnecessary. If your sentence makes sense without them, get rid of them: “He recently discovered that both the UI and WSU currently have lunchrooms” should be: “He discovered UI and WSU have lunchrooms.” 47. Up. Do not use up as a verb. 48. Who, whom. A tough one, but generally you are safe to use whom to refer to someone who has been the object of an action. Who is the word when somebody has been the actor. Right: A 19-year-old woman, to whom the room was rented, left the window open. Right: A 19-year-old woman, who rented the room, left the window open. Add anything as you need it.Argonaut Style Guide
